transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-28
Start: 14:05 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Roberts (Redwood SE), Oliver Grant (CISO, Coppergate), Priya Menon (Head of Data), Jonas Keller (Platform), Ava Li (Legal)

Summary (auto):
Coppergate is evaluating Redwood for event-driven underwriting assistants and redaction-sensitive KYC workflows. Primary concerns — strong tenant isolation, demonstrable audit evidence for finance auditors, strict log retention and redaction, and encryption key residency. Looking at hosted vs. dedicated vs. private and tradeoffs between speed-to-deploy and auditability.

Topics:
- Tenant isolation model (logical vs physical)
- Audit artifact generation and evidence workflow
- KMS residency & key rotation proofs
- Log redaction & retention policies
- Compliance fit: SOC2 / PCI / GDPR interaction

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for making time, really quick intros, im Maya chen, AE, and with me is Ethan our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Oliver (Coppergate): hey yeah thanks, this is Oliver, CISO. we'll go over our needs. we moved a bunch of inference toward vendor APIs but auditors flagged the inability to prove end-to-end isolation between tenants.
[00:25] Ethan (Redwood): yeah totally, thanks. quick question to scope — are you more concerned about cryptographic separation of keys or physical separation of compute for audit evidence? or both?
[00:40] Oliver: both, but if pushed we need cryptographic separation first. auditors want to see "who had access to which requests" and a chain of custody. we also have PCI scope for payments metadata, and GDPR PII concerns for EU customers, so redaction is required before storing logs.
[01:05] Priya: and to add, our legal team needs a reproducible report we can hand to auditors, not just a collection of logs. e.g. a PDF with access timeline, key id, and hashes of prompt/response objects where appropriate.
[01:22] Maya: ok great, high-level we support three deployment modes — hosted, dedicated reserved pools, and private VPC/on-prem. for the strongest evidence and isolation you typically see customers pick dedicated or private. hosted can be configured with tenant-aware encryption but auditors sometimes require physically isolated tenancy.
[01:42] Jonas: can you clarifiy what you mean by tenant-aware encryption? do you mean per-tenant KMS keys?
[01:48] Ethan: yeah we call it per-tenant CMKs — customer-managed keys — where each tenant's data is encrypted with a distinct key. in private mode the control plane for keys stays with you, and logs that are generated are limited to metadata you choose. in dedicated mode we can provide dedicated GPU pools and optional customer-managed KMS with key material in your cloud KMS.
[02:12] Ava (Legal): will Redwood provide key rotation proofs and attestations? auditors want evidence rotation happened on schedule with derivative key ids recorded.
[02:20] Ethan: yes we can export key-rotation events. we'll log rotation start/finish, key id snapshots, and provide signed records. there's an artefact export function — redwood calls them audit bundles — which include signed event lists and a digest of the stored artifacts.
[02:38] Oliver: how granular are those bundles though? can we see request-level linkage? i'm worried about linking a tokenized request back to PII — we want the ability to show hashes only, and to redact the raw message text.
[02:52] Maya: good point. we support configurable redaction pipelines before any persistent logs are written. redaction rules can be provided as patterns or via a small normalizer function you run in your environment. the audit bundle can contain salted hashes of the original prompt so auditors can verify integrity without exposing raw PII.
[03:14] Priya: salt management then becomes sensitive; where's the salt stored? if it's within Redwood hosted, that defeats the purpose.
[03:22] Ethan: correct. in private/dedicated setups the salt/peppers can be customer-controlled — either in their KMS or a vault — so only you can derive original content. in hosted mode we offer an option to use your KMS via external key wrapping, but that still leaves some metadata in Redwood control plane unless you select private.
[03:44] Jonas: also interested in network isolation. for private deployment, do we get an air-gapped option or just VPC peering and strict egress rules?
[03:52] Maya: we have both paths. on-prem package is air-gappable; VPC private deployment uses customer VPC with strict egress ACLs, security groups, and optional transit gateway. we can also do static egress IPs for firewall allowlists.
[04:08] Oliver: auditors also want to see RBAC changes, who escalated, who requested keys. will your audit bundle include admin actions from the control plane?
[04:18] Ethan: yes, admin ops — role grants, RBAC changes, API key creation/deletion, and model rollouts — are captured in control-plane audit logs. For private installs we provide the raw control-plane logs and an index file that maps actions to user ids; for hosted we ship event digests with certified signatures.
[04:38] Priya: what's your retention policy flexibility? we need 7 years for some payment artifacts, but we want to keep raw prompts for 90 days only. can you scoping retention per artifact class?
[04:52] Maya: yes you can configure retention per artifact type — e.g., prompt_text: 90d, prompt_hash: 7y, access_audit: 7y. for hosted accounts we also can set automatic expiration and nearline archival; for private you control storage lifecycles.
[05:08] Oliver: are the long-lived hashes reversible? if an auditor requests to replay the prompt back with your salt, can they derive it?
[05:16] Ethan: not reversible without the salt and KMS. that's the whole point. in our recommended flow, the customer manages the salt and only provides auditors a secure, temporary environment to validate a hash if absolutely required.
[05:30] Ava: on evidence packaging — will redwood produce a single PDF or do we get a machine-readable bundle? auditors want both: human-readable overview + machine attestations.
[05:40] Maya: audit bundles include a human-readable summary PDF, CSVs of event timelines, and a signed machine-readable JSONL of events. again, customers can choose which components are persisted in Redwood vs exported directly to their S3.
[05:54] Jonas: does the JSONL include token-level latencies or just request metadata?
[05:58] Ethan: request metadata only by default (timestamps, model id, key id, tenant id, duration). token-level traces are available as an opt-in debug stream for a short window and only if enabled — usually for performance debugging, not for auditor consumption.
[06:16] Oliver: what about model fallbacks/emergency? if you route to a lower-cost model in failover, does that appear in the control-plane traces? auditors will ask why a customer saw different outputs at times.
[06:28] Ethan: yes failover events are logged as part of the request trace and included in the audit bundle. you can see routing decision, reason code (capacity/fallback/latency), and target model id.
[06:40] Priya: encryption-in-transit — do you support TLS mutual auth between our services and Redwood?
[06:44] Maya: mTLS is supported for private and dedicated endpoints; hosted supports strong TLS with client cert rotation for certain enterprise tiers.
[06:54] Ava: any certifications you have out of the box?
[06:56] Ethan: we publish our SOC2 Type II report, and for payments several customers pair our platform with their PCI attestation. Redwood itself is not a PCI certifier, but we provide the controls and evidence to support your PCI audit. we also maintain data-processing addendums for GDPR and help with DPIA artifacts.
[07:16] Oliver: question on geography — we need a full EU-resident stack for EU customers and cannot replicate logs outside EU. can you lock audit bundles to region?
[07:25] Maya: yes, region-locking is standard for private and available for dedicated reservations in supported cloud regions; for hosted we can route EU tenant traffic to EU regions but some control-plane metadata may still be US-based unless you select a EU-dedicated plan.
[07:42] Jonas: for evidence workflow, our internal auditor requires a signature chain. you mentioned signed bundles — what's the signing mechanism?
[07:50] Ethan: we sign bundles with an HSM-backed service key; in private installs you can swap in your own signing key from your HSM. the bundle includes canonicalized JSON and a detached signature so you can verify integrity independently.
[08:06] Priya: ok helps. could you also describe the process we go through to generate an auditor packet? stepwise?
[08:12] Maya: sure — step 1: decide deployment (hosted/dedicated/private). step 2: configure retention/redaction policies and per-tenant CMKs. step 3: enable audit bundle exports to your S3 (or we provide temporary download). step 4: run a test export for a sample timeframe and provide it to your auditor; step 5: once accepted, we can automate scheduled exports and produce a signed monthly packet.
[08:36] Oliver: timeline wise, we're aiming to pick a vendor and start a pilot in Q1. security sign-off is the gating factor.
[08:44] Ava: small point — legal will need to see deletion proofs if requested under GDPR (right to be forgotten) — how do you prove deletion?
[08:52] Ethan: we issue deletion receipts with a deletion job id, target artifact types, and a post-deletion verification digest showing artifact no longer present. for long-term archival like hashed artifacts we can show removal of link indexes. in private mode you can run a forensic scan to prove zero bits but that's on-prem.
[09:10] Priya: anything else around multi-tenant caching? concerns that KV cache might leak tokens between tenants.
[09:18] Maya: cache is strictly sharded by tenant id; we also support per-tenant cache namespaces or disabled caching per route if you need absolute determinism. there is a short window of live cache but it's never shared across tenant namespaces.
[09:32] Jonas: would you allow us to run a PoC where we inject synthetic PII and attempt to prove it's not leaked?
[09:38] Maya: absolutely, that's a common POC. we can set up a dedicated pool, give you the audit bundle for the POC window, and walk through the auditor packet creation.
[09:48] Oliver: costs — what extra costs for dedicated/private and for audit-bundle exports?
[09:54] Maya: dedicated has a steady reservation price plus per-token usage; private has a platform license. audit bundle exports and long-term archival have modest fees due to storage and signing processes — we'll provide a pricing sheet.
[10:06] Ava: one more compliance nuance — if auditors want raw logs for a subpoena, how do you handle that?
[10:12] Ethan: subpoenas go through our legal team and customer legal; we can provide raw logs only per the contract and with appropriate NDAs and legal processes. for EU data we adhere to data transfer restrictions.
[10:26] Maya: ok jumping to wrap up — recap and next steps?
[10:30] Maya: we'll share our SOC2, the architecture diagram for private deployment, an example audit bundle (sanitized), and the KMS residency note. we'll propose a security deep dive with your infra team first week of Jan.
[10:44] Oliver: sounds good, Priya will send retention rules and a point-of-contact for auditors.
[10:50] Priya: yes i'll send that by Jan 5.
[10:54] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and a proposed calendar invite.
[11:00] Meeting end (rough).

Notes on transcript quality: speaker overlap minimal, occasional ASR confusion of acronyms (e.g., "kay vee cache" for KV cache, "sam-el" for SAML).
